figures.caption: Table 13: Comparison on the RepoAudit benchmark. TP numbers for RepoAudit are published by Guo et al. and include both GT-matched bugs and additional discoveries. For SPECA, we omit an aggregate TP count because computing it requires estimating GT matches—an inherently approximate procedure. Recall is not reported because the GT was constructed from RepoAudit’s own discoveries. 𝑏New candidates = author-validated bugs beyond the established GT (Level D validation, see Appendix D).

Figure 4: Findings per issue: the property neighborhood effect. Eleven of 15 matched issues are covered by two or more complementary properties, explaining both the high recall and the gap between finding-level and cluster-level precision.
Figure 5: Property family to ground truth issue flow. The horizontal density around a handful of issues visualizes the property neighborhood effect.
Figure 3: Phase 5 (Audit) vs Phase 6 (FP Filter). Phase 6 improves precision from 56.9% to 66.7% while preserving 100% recall on H/M/L findings, raising F1 from 72.5% to 80.0%.

Figure 8: Tool precision on theRepoAudit benchmark. SPECA (Sonnet 4.5)matches the best RepoAudit configuration (88.9%) while also surfacing 12 author-validated candidate bugs beyond the established ground truth.

Figure 1: The SPECA pipeline. Phases 1–3 (Knowledge Structuring) derive security properties from specifications; Phases 4–6 (Systematic Auditing) verify properties against implementations. In multi-implementation settings, the left stage executes once and the right stage executes per target.
Table 3: The four property types in SPECA’s vocabulary.
Figure 19: Bug detection matrix (40 total bugs: 35 nondisputed ground truth, 5 disputed).

Figure 14: False-positive root-cause taxonomy with pipelinephase origins (N=16 deeply analyzed from 44 total FPs; see Table 9). The three causes each map to a distinct pipeline phase, making the failure surface structurally analyzable.

Figure 13: Issue × property family TP finding counts (postreview). The property neighborhood effect is visible as horizontal bands where a single issue is detected by multiple complementary properties; shared vertical structure across repositories reflects the cross-implementation comparability the property vocabulary enables.

Figure 7: Phase 6 three-gate FP filter effectiveness (N=30 DISPUTED_FP). The three retained gates each target a narrow, mechanically verifiable condition, preserving H/M/L recall while filtering roughly two-thirds of flagged false positives.

Figure 2: Phase 5 audit flow for a single property. Each property undergoes three sub-phases:Map (decompose assertion into sub-claims), Prove (verify each sub-claim against code), and Stress-Test (validate or challenge the conclusion).

Table 15: Accounting reconciliation of all finding counts reported in RQ1. Each count traces to a single partition so that the precision numerator/denominator and FP-analysis population can be verified by a reader.

Figure 12: SPECA output quality breakdown (N=102). Of 102 pre-review findings, 48 are security-relevant in the final output, 24 are confirmed FPs, 20 are correctly filtered by Phase 6, and 10 are TPs lost to Phase 6 filtering.
